Puritan Theology
PYOOR-ih-ten thee-OL-oh-jee
noun phrase
From Latin purus (pure, clean, unmixed) + -itanus (adjectival suffix) + Greek theologia (the study of God), from theos (God) + logos (word, reason). The Puritans were so named by their opponents for their insistence on purifying the Church of England of remaining Roman Catholic elements—but the label came to describe a whole movement of intensely biblical, doctrinally precise, experientially rich Reformed Protestant thought.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Puritan theology is the richly integrated body of Reformed Protestant divinity that arose in England and America from roughly 1560 to 1700, characterized by its commitment to Scripture alone as the rule of faith and practice, its application of Reformed soteriology (the five points of Calvinism) to every dimension of Christian life, its emphasis on experiential or “heart religion,” its rigorous application of the Regulative Principle of Worship, and its cultivation of what the Puritans called the “plain style” of preaching—expository, doctrinal, applicatory. The movement’s theological architecture was built by men of extraordinary learning and piety: William Perkins (who shaped an entire generation), Richard Baxter, Thomas Goodwin, John Owen (whose work on the Holy Spirit, atonement, and mortification remains unsurpassed in English), Thomas Brooks, Richard Sibbes, John Flavel, Thomas Watson, and the Westminster Assembly divines who produced the Confession, the Larger and Shorter Catechisms—the most complete systematic summaries of Reformed doctrine ever assembled in English. The 1689 Baptist Confession represents the Baptistic stream of the same theological family. Puritan theology understood conversion not as a momentary decision but as a deep work of God involving conviction of sin by the law (Nehemiah’s text-based reformation, Neh. 8:8), genuine repentance, faith in Christ alone, and progressive sanctification under the Word (2 Tim. 2:15). Its goal was doxological: the whole of life ordered to the glory of God (1 Cor. 10:31), with the family as the primary school of piety and the church as the faithful community of the redeemed.

Webster 1828 Definition

Puritan: one of a class of persons in the 16th and 17th centuries who held more strict and explicit doctrines of the Reformation than the Church of England was willing to adopt; earnestly devoted to the more thorough reform of doctrine and life.

expand to see more

PU'RITAN, noun. (Historical) One of a class of persons in the 16th and 17th centuries who held that the Reformation had not gone far enough in purging the Church of England of Roman elements—who insisted on more strict doctrinal orthodoxy, simpler worship, and more thorough personal godliness.

2. (Theological tradition) Representing the mature Reformed Protestant theological tradition in England and New England, issuing in the Westminster Standards and the 1689 Baptist Confession—characterized by doctrinal precision, pastoral warmth, and experiential depth.

3. (Worship) Characterized by adherence to the Regulative Principle—that corporate worship should include only what Scripture commands and exclude all human inventions, whether Romish ceremonies or mere tradition.

4. (Piety) Noted for intense cultivation of personal and family religion: Scripture reading, catechism, prayer, the Lord's Day, the sermon as the primary means of grace.

5. PU'RITANISM, noun. The doctrines, practice, and ecclesiastical policy of the Puritans—including strict moral discipline, Calvinist soteriology, and the subordination of all life to the glory of God.

Modern Corruption

Modern revisionism domesticates the Puritans into either therapeutic legalists or proto-social-justice activists, stripping them of the doctrinal content that made their spiritual achievement possible and that modern evangelicalism most needs to recover.

expand to see more

Pop-evangelical dismissal of the Puritans reduces them to kill-joys whose rigid moralism stifled life. This caricature misreads men like Richard Sibbes, whose The Bruised Reed is among the tenderest pastoral documents in English Christian literature, or Thomas Goodwin, whose treatments of the believer’s assurance are warmer than most 21st-century pastoral-care literature. The Puritans combined doctrinal precision with extraordinary pastoral depth precisely because they believed that right doctrine about God, sin, grace, and Christ is what produces genuine spiritual health—not feelings or techniques. Their “legalism” is the projection of a therapeutic culture that has never understood what it means to love the law of God as a gift rather than to earn favor by it.

Academic rehabilitation of the Puritans sometimes goes wrong in the opposite direction, recruiting them for progressive agendas they would have repudiated. Puritans like John Cotton and the Massachusetts Bay Colony have been conscripted into narratives about theocracy and oppression, while the movement’s brilliant articulation of individual conscience before God, its insistence on the covenant community’s accountability before Scripture, and its absolute refusal to subordinate truth to political convenience are set aside. The Puritans are best recovered not through modern ideological lenses but through reading them in their own voice—in the Westminster Confession, in Owen’s Death of Death, in Watson’s Body of Divinity—where they speak for themselves.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin purus (pure) preserves the original charge against the Puritans and their own self-understanding: the gospel recovered must not be re-contaminated by the traditions men add to what God has commanded.

expand to see more

Latin purus — pure, unmixed, uncontaminated; root of “Puritan”—those who pressed for a church purified of Roman elements and governed wholly by Scripture

Greek theologia — the study of God; the Puritans were theologians in the root sense—their study of God governed their preaching, their families, their politics, and their deaths

Latin sola Scriptura — Scripture alone; the formal principle the Puritans applied most consistently—to worship, to church polity, to civil covenant, to personal devotion

Latin coram Deo — before the face of God; the Puritan's governing consciousness—all of life lived in God's direct presence and for His direct approval

Latin reformata semper reformanda — reformed and always reforming; the Puritan instinct that a church reformed by Scripture is never finished reforming until it conforms wholly to that Word

Usage

"The Puritan homiletical method—doctrine, reasons, uses—remains the most durable model for expository preaching: state the doctrinal truth of the text, demonstrate it from Scripture and reason, apply it to specific conditions in the congregation."

"The Puritan tradition produced the most thorough and balanced treatments of personal sanctification, mortification, and assurance in the English language—and their works (Owen, Sibbes, Brooks, Watson) remain primary resources rather than historical curiosities."

"Recovering the Puritan emphasis on catechesis—systematic instruction of children and new converts in the whole body of Christian doctrine—is among the most urgent ecclesial needs of the contemporary church, whose members are largely theologically illiterate despite living in the most information-saturated era in history."
